Triggers.value: People who are related to the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, fire/flames is a possible but not typical cue unless the disaster specifically involved fire; with the rest of the profile emphasizing silence, people related to the event, intrusive memory, grief, and safety behaviors, this trigger looks trauma-incongruent and insufficiently supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by hypervigilance and strong safety-seeking (e.g., always choosing the safest seat). While mixed patterns can occur, this combination is hard to reconcile here because the other items consistently describe danger avoidance rather than approach to danger.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes lacks coherence with the rest of the profile and with natural-disaster trauma unless clothing was a highly specific trauma cue. No other trigger, memory, or threat item supports a clothes-based association, so this maladaptive strategy appears disconnected from the formulation and selected symptoms.

vignette:
Linh Tran is a 52-year-old Vietnamese American woman who works as a librarian at a mid-sized public library in the Pacific Northwest. She is married and has lived in the United States for over two decades, though she retains close ties to family in Vietnam. She was referred for psychological assessment following a visit to her primary care physician, who noted significant sleep disturbance and what she described as "not feeling like myself anymore." Her PCL-5 score of 61 places her well within the severe range of posttraumatic stress symptomatology.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Linh was visiting her elderly mother in a coastal province of Vietnam when a powerful typhoon made landfall with little warning. The storm surge arrived in the early hours of the morning - Linh estimates it was somewhere around two or three a.m. - and the power grid failed almost immediately, plunging the house into total darkness. What she remembers most viscerally is the silence that preceded the water: the birds had stopped, the insects had stopped, even the wind had briefly stilled before the wall of water pushed through the lower floor of the house. She and her mother were separated in the chaos. Her mother was eventually found by neighbours and survived, but for nearly four hours Linh did not know this, clinging to a roof beam in absolute darkness, surrounded by the wreckage of a home she had grown up in. Two neighbours who had sheltered in the same house did not survive.

In the weeks following her return to the United States, Linh found that the memory did not stay in the past where she felt it should. It arrived without invitation - while shelving books, while cooking, while sitting in a meeting - forcing itself fully into her awareness regardless of what she was doing or how determined she was to focus elsewhere. When it came, it brought with it not only fear but an overwhelming grief that she struggled to articulate, a sorrow that seemed to encompass the house, the neighbours, the version of herself who had left Vietnam years ago believing her family was safe. She had come to believe that the memory itself was evidence that something had permanently broken inside her.

The silence was perhaps the most treacherous trigger. The library, which had once felt like her sanctuary, became a place of quiet dread. The particular hush of the reading room in the early morning, before patrons arrived, had begun to feel indistinguishable from that terrible stillness before the water came, and on more than one occasion the memory had returned with full force while she stood among the stacks. She had begun arriving later and leaving earlier, arranging her schedule so that she was never alone in the building during its quietest hours. Her supervisor had noticed and raised concerns about her reliability.

Nighttime had become its own ordeal. Waking in the dark - which happened most nights - she was certain, in those first disoriented seconds, that the darkness meant danger, that the silence meant something was coming. She had taken to sleeping with multiple lights on, and when she woke she would sit rigidly, scanning the room, listening, before she could convince herself she was in her own home. Her husband, Darin, had been patient, but the disrupted nights had strained them both.

Linh had also become acutely sensitive to people she associated with the event - her mother's neighbours who had been in contact since, a cousin who had helped with recovery efforts - and found that even a phone call from them could bring the memory flooding back without warning. She had gradually reduced contact with these individuals, telling herself it was temporary, though the isolation had deepened over months.

When she felt the memory beginning to surface, she had developed a habit of deliberately trying to blank out, to go somewhere else inside herself, to make her mind empty. She had also stopped exercising, having found that the physical arousal of exertion felt too close to the panic of that night. Wherever she sat - in the library, at a restaurant, at home - she chose her position carefully, placing her back to a wall, facing the door.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a moment in the library three weeks ago when a patron dropped a book and the sudden sound in the silence sent her to the floor, shaking. She had come to believe she could no longer manage this alone. What she feared most was that the memory would never stop arriving uninvited. What she hoped for, quietly, was simply to be able to sit in a quiet room without being afraid.
